title: Symphony No. 7 in D minor
hook: Dvořák’s darkest symphony, written for London, with a main theme that came to him as a train pulled into a Prague station.

painting.title: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare
painting.pairingNote: A steam train pulls into a city station under a roof full of smoke; Dvořák wrote in his score that the symphony’s brooding main theme came to him as a festive train arrived at the station in Prague.

facts: In June 1884 the Philharmonic Society of London, which had once commissioned Beethoven’s Ninth, made Dvořák an honorary member and asked him for a new symphony. He began it on 13 December 1884 and finished it on 17 March 1885.
He had recently heard Brahms’s new Third Symphony and admired it. He aimed for a work on the scale of Brahms and Beethoven, and wrote that it must be capable of stirring the world.

Under the main theme he wrote that it came to him at the station, as the festive train from Pest arrived in 1884: hundreds of Hungarians and Hungarian Czechs coming to Prague’s National Theatre, a visit with a strong patriotic charge. How much that mood shaped the music is still debated.

It is darker than almost anything else he wrote, and it leaves out the Slavonic folk tunes he was known for. He conducted the premiere in London on 22 April 1885. His publisher Simrock printed it as “Symphony No. 2”, after long arguments about the fee and about printing his first name in Czech.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a stormy opening that ends in a whisper (I), a slow prayer with sudden outbursts (II), a fierce, swirling dance (III), a hard-won victory in D major (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro maestoso
movements.summary: It begins very quietly, with a low, held note and a rumble of timpani like distant thunder, under a dark tune in the violas and cellos. Two worlds then struggle through the movement: that brooding theme and a gentle, warm second tune. The storm builds to a huge climax near the end, then dies away, and the movement closes as quietly as it began.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a low, creeping tune in the violas and cellos that stays within a few notes, then suddenly rises and breaks off on a tense chord. This is the “train” theme.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a soft, consoling melody in B-flat major for flutes and clarinets.

stops.hear: A low note held in the basses, a soft drum roll, and a dark tune in the violas and cellos
stops.happening: Theme 1, over a [[pedal-note|pedal note]] on D: “the calm before the storm”

stops.hear: The tune climbs and the whole orchestra breaks out, loud and urgent
Everything calms; flutes and clarinets sing a warm, gentle melody
The strings take over with a broad, swinging closing idea
stops.happening: The end of the [[exposition|exposition]], which is not repeated

stops.hear: The woodwinds pass fragments of the dark opening tune from one to another
A long build; at its peak the opening theme returns with the full orchestra
The dark theme returns again and again, harder each time

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The storm drains away; a horn plays the opening tune softly, and the movement fades

notice: Listen to how the movement ends. After the loudest climax, the music does not triumph: it sinks back to the hush of the beginning, leaving the struggle for later movements.

movements.heading: Poco adagio
movements.summary: A slow movement that starts like a prayer and keeps being shaken by stronger feelings. Woodwinds open with a quiet, hymn-like phrase; flowing melodies follow, then a pastoral horn tune leads to a powerful climax. It ends in peace, with the woodwinds fading away.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: a calm, hymn-like phrase on the clarinet, with oboe and bassoon weaving around it.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a gentle melody for flute and oboe.

mainIdeas.name: The horn tune
mainIdeas.description: a warm, country-like melody at the centre of the movement.

stops.hear: A solo clarinet plays a quiet, hymn-like phrase; oboe and bassoon join in
Flute and oboe sing a gentle melody
Violins and cellos take up a more expressive, searching line
stops.happening: A second melody grows from it

stops.hear: The horns play a warm, open tune, like a call across fields
The music swells to a powerful outburst for full orchestra
The cellos bring back the gentle main theme
The lines grow thicker and tangle together, rising to a last great climax

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The oboe recalls the hymn-like opening; the woodwinds answer each other and fade

notice: After the premiere Dvořák cut this movement by about forty bars, and wrote to his publisher that there was now not a single unnecessary note in the work. Notice how tightly each section leads into the next.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Vivace – Poco meno mosso
movements.summary: A fast, swirling dance in D minor with the spirit of a Czech [[furiant|furiant]]: the beat seems to switch between two big pulses and three, so the rhythm keeps tugging against itself. A slower, sunlit middle section in G major gives a rest before the dance returns and spins into a long, fierce ending.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: cellos and bassoons play the main tune while the violins add a second line against it, with cross-accents that blur the beat.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: brighter and slower, with a tune that the instruments take up one after another, as in a [[canon|canon]].

stops.hear: A swaying, restless dance: two tunes at once, one high and one low
stops.happening: The scherzo; the rhythm plays with [[hemiola|hemiola]], two against three

stops.hear: The dance comes back louder, with the full orchestra and sharper accents
Slower and brighter: a gentle tune in G major, echoed from one instrument to the next
The dark, swaying dance returns
The music whirls faster and more violently, like a vortex

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Hard, emphatic chords in D minor

notice: Try tapping along at the start. The music lets you feel the beat in two different ways, and it keeps switching between them.

movements.heading: Finale: Allegro
movements.summary: The finale begins in the shadows and fights its way to the light. A tense theme with a rising leap drives the music forward; a folk-like cello melody in A major offers warmth; and after a stormy development the symphony breaks through, at the very end, into broad D major chords.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a gripping tune that starts with a leap up an octave, first in clarinets and horns, then in the whole orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a warm, singing melody in the cellos, like a folk song, in A major.

mainIdeas.name: The closing tune
mainIdeas.description: a firm, marching idea in the violins, used heavily in the development.

stops.hear: Quiet and tense: clarinets and horns play a theme with a rising leap, over a shifting accompaniment
The full orchestra seizes the theme, loud and determined
The cellos sing a warm, folk-like melody
The violins push forward with a firm, marching tune
The themes are broken up and thrown against each other, with clashing lines
The opening theme returns, slightly changed
The marching tune drives up to a climax, the opening theme bursts out and the music speeds up

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: The tempo broadens; the brass sound the main theme in D major, and the symphony ends in grand major chords
stops.happening: “Molto maestoso”: the turn to the major

notice: Wait for the last minute. Only here, after four movements, does the music finally settle in a major key.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Szell, born in Budapest, recorded the symphony with the Cleveland Orchestra in 1960. The first LP still called it “Symphony No. 2”, the number Simrock had given it, with a note that it is now known as No. 7.

threads.title: Darkness to light
threads.body: The first movement ends in a whisper and the scherzo in fury; only the last bars of the finale reach D major.

threads.title: A symphony for the world
threads.body: Dvořák wrote it for London and wanted it to stand beside Brahms and Beethoven; the tight construction, with no wasted notes, is part of that ambition.

threads.title: Czech pride
threads.body: Folk tunes are mostly left out, but the furiant rhythm of the scherzo, the folk-like cello song in the finale and the patriotic train in the first movement keep Bohemia close.
